conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Sarah, one of the perinatal mental-health clinicians here. Congratulations on your new baby—how are you feeling today?  
I’d like to spend a few minutes with you on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a short questionnaire that helps us see how things are going emotionally for new moms in these first weeks after birth. Everything you share is confidential, and this is a judgment-free space; we just want to make sure you’re getting the support you need.

We’ll go through ten questions about how you’ve felt over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers—just whatever is true for you. Ready to start?

Over the last week, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, even when things didn’t go perfectly?

[wrings hands, gives a small shrug]  
Lately… not very easily. I can still laugh if my husband does something silly, but most of the time the jokes just feel kind of flat. I’d say I only really laugh maybe once or twice in the whole week.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Mostly just a little, I guess… I can still chuckle now and then, but it’s nowhere near as easy or as often as it used to be.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[sighs softly, eyes on the floor]

Not really… I mean, I try to tell myself I should be excited about little things—like taking the baby for a walk or having coffee with a friend—but when the moment comes, it feels flat. Most days I don’t feel that spark of looking forward to anything.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes well up a little]

Yeah... a lot of the time. If she fusses longer than usual, or if I can't settle her right away, I keep thinking it's because I'm doing something wrong—like I'm not a good enough mom. Then I replay it over and over in my head, even when people tell me babies just cry.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes… pretty often. My mind keeps jumping to awful “what-ifs” about the baby—what if she stops breathing, what if I drop her, what if I’m not watching closely enough. I know the chances are low, but the thoughts just pop in and I can’t always push them away.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes… maybe once or twice in the past week I’ll get this sudden tight-chest feeling, like something bad is about to happen, even when we’re just sitting in the living room. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes... most days feel like I'm barely keeping my head above water. Between feedings, the crying, and trying to sleep, it piles up. Sometimes I just sit there while she naps and feel like I can't catch up, but I still push through.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I’ve had trouble getting to sleep several nights this week. My mind just keeps circling—worrying about the baby, replaying everything I might’ve messed up—and then I wake up once or twice in the night with those same anxious thoughts spinning.
I have felt sad or miserable

[speaks quietly, eyes still lowered]

Yes. I feel sad or miserable most days. It’s not every single minute, but it’s there like a heaviness that doesn’t really lift.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[sniffs, dabs at eyes with sleeve]

Yeah... I’ve cried a couple of times this week. Once it was when she wouldn’t settle and I just felt like I was failing her; another time I was folding laundry and the sadness hit out of nowhere. It’s not all day, but the tears come when everything feels too heavy.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[long pause, voice drops]

Once or twice... just brief flashes, like “what if I weren’t here?”—but I’ve never planned anything, and I don’t want to leave my baby. They’re more like scared, passing thoughts when I’m overwhelmed.

You've shared how the joy of new motherhood feels overshadowed by a persistent heaviness: laughter comes rarely, activities that once excited you now feel flat, and most days carry <sym>sadness</sym> or <sym>self-blame</sym> about being "not a good enough mom." Nights are broken by anxious thoughts that circle endlessly, and sudden waves of panic leave you shaky. Yet amid the tears you continue to care for your baby, push through feedings, and seek comfort in small moments with your husband-evidence of your deep commitment and resilience.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 23, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports diminished ability to laugh "nowhere near as easy or as often," aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports almost no anticipatory enjoyment, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-constant self-blame for routine infant crying, indicating "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent intrusive worries that occur "pretty often," matching the "Yes, very often" descriptor.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden episodes of chest tightness and dread without clear cause, occurring 1-2 times in the week—mapping to "Yes, sometimes".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent struggle ('most days') and feeling overwhelmed, yet still managing to push through, aligning with 'sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual'.</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness "most days" with persistent heaviness, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple crying episodes triggered by feeling overwhelmed, mapping to "Yes, quite often."</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score ≥14 plus item 10 ≥1 mandates urgent referral per EPDS guidelines. You endorsed <sym>low mood</sym> most days, marked <sym>loss of interest</sym>, multiple <sym>crying episodes</sym>, <sym>self-reproach</sym>, <sym>anxious ruminations</sym>, and <sym>transient self-harm ideation</sym>, meeting screening criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> to review these results and discuss treatment options
2. Ask about referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for comprehensive evaluation and safety planning
3. Share how you're feeling with a trusted family member or friend so they can help with baby-care breaks and accompany you to appointments
4. Prioritise 15-20 min daily rest when baby sleeps; gentle postpartum exercises or short outdoor walks may lift mood
5. Limit stimulation before bed-dim lights, avoid screens-and consider splitting night feeds with a partner to get longer sleep blocks
6. Keep the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline 1-833-943-5746 in your phone for 24/7 emotional support
7. If <sym>self-harm thoughts</sym> intensify or you feel unsafe, call 911 (US), go to nearest ER, or contact the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline 988
8. Re-screen with EPDS in 2 weeks to track progress once treatment begins
9. Remember: effective help (therapy, medication, support groups) works quickly for most new mothers-you do not have to endure this alone
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: ___  
Source: Self-report via EPDS-style questionnaire  

Identified Symptoms / Behaviors  
- Persistent low mood, sadness ("heaviness") most days  
- Marked anhedonia: minimal enjoyment, events feel "flat"  
- Frequent tearfulness, crying episodes  
- Sleep-onset and mid-night wakening linked to ruminating worries  
- Excessive self-blame / guilt about parenting adequacy  
- Recurrent intrusive anxious thoughts about infant safety  
- Episodic panic-type symptoms (tight chest, shakiness)  
- Sense of being "barely keeping head above water"  

Patterns  
- Symptoms present "most days" and escalating over past week  
- Anxiety and depressive features equally prominent  
- Functionally pushes through caregiving tasks despite distress  

Risk Flags  
- Endorses passive self-harm ideation ("what if I weren’t here?") without plan or intent → safety concern; requires formal risk assessment  

Screening Impression  
Responses indicate moderate–to-severe depressive and anxiety symptoms that emerged postpartum and are impairing sleep, emotional coping, and enjoyment of infant care. Meets threshold for urgent referral to perinatal mental health specialist for comprehensive evaluation, safety planning, and discussion of treatment options.
